clinicalPearls: A congenital defect in the posterior partition between the larynx or trachea and the oesophagus, allowing communication and consequent aspiration
Presents in infancy with feeding-related coughing and choking, recurrent chest infections, stridor, and cyanotic episodes
Severity is graded by the inferior extent of the cleft, from an interarytenoid defect to an extensive laryngotracheo-oesophageal cleft
Frequently associated with other anomalies, including tracheo-oesophageal fistula and syndromes such as Opitz-Frias and VACTERL/Pallister-Hall
Diagnosis rests on rigid endoscopy under anaesthesia with active probing of the interarytenoid region, as shallow clefts are easily missed
Minor clefts may be managed conservatively with feeding modification and reflux measures, while deeper clefts require endoscopic or open surgical repair
Aspiration risk makes airway protection and nutrition the immediate priorities in a symptomatic infant
reference.pathophysiology: A laryngeal cleft results from failure of the posterior cricoid lamina and the tracheo-oesophageal septum to fuse during embryogenesis, leaving an abnormal midline communication between the airway posteriorly and the digestive tract. The deficient partition removes the normal separation that protects the airway during swallowing, so liquids and secretions spill directly into the larynx and trachea. The degree of aspiration and respiratory compromise parallels the depth of the cleft, ranging from occasional aspiration with a shallow interarytenoid defect to life-threatening soiling of the airway and recurrent pneumonia with an extensive cleft reaching the carina.
additionalDifferentials: Neurological (central or bulbar) dysphagia with aspiration
additionalInvestigations: Rigid microlaryngoscopy and bronchoscopy with probing of the interarytenoid area, the diagnostic gold standard
Flexible fibreoptic laryngoscopy for initial airway assessment
Functional endoscopic or videofluoroscopic swallow study to document aspiration
Contrast swallow to define the tracheo-oesophageal anatomy
Screening for associated anomalies given the syndromic associations
redFlags: Cyanotic or apnoeic episodes during feeding
Recurrent aspiration pneumonia and failure to thrive
Severe stridor or respiratory distress in a neonate
A deep cleft extending into the trachea, which is life-threatening and demands urgent airway protection
reference.prognosis: Shallow clefts often do well with conservative feeding and reflux management, and repaired clefts generally have a good outcome, but deep laryngotracheo-oesophageal clefts carry substantial morbidity and mortality, especially where associated anomalies coexist.
pitfalls: Missing a shallow interarytenoid cleft because it was not actively probed during endoscopy
Attributing feeding-related symptoms solely to reflux and delaying definitive assessment
Overlooking associated congenital anomalies that alter management
Underestimating aspiration risk and permitting unmodified oral feeding in a symptomatic infant
references: Cummings Otolaryngology: Head and Neck Surgery
Scott-Brown's Otorhinolaryngology, Head and Neck Surgery
management: Match treatment to cleft depth: manage shallow interarytenoid clefts conservatively with thickened feeds and feeding modification, and repair deeper clefts endoscopically or by open cervical/thoracic approach
Control gastro-oesophageal reflux with anti-reflux measures and acid-suppressing therapy to reduce airway soiling and protect any repair
Optimise feeding with speech-and-language-led swallow therapy and adjusted feed consistency to minimise aspiration
Treat recurrent aspiration pneumonia promptly with appropriate antimicrobials and respiratory support
Monitor with serial swallow assessment and respiratory review, and re-endoscope to confirm healing after repair
Screen for associated anomalies such as tracheo-oesophageal fistula, VACTERL, Opitz-Frias, and Pallister-Hall given the syndromic associations
Coordinate paediatric ENT, gastroenterology, respiratory, and speech-and-language teams
